contributions.statement: Before adopting a model router or cascade, report three numbers on a held-out split: the oracle gap with a selection-valid lower bound, the router's held-out gain over the best single model, and a simultaneous interval over every router variant tried. If the gain's lower bound is zero, keep the single best model.
contributions.evidence: §4 Theorems 4 and 6; §7.1 Tables 1-2: oracle gaps certified positive on all four tasks while the best-of-11 router gain has lower limit .000 on all four.

contributions.statement: A large oracle gap across a model pool does not mean a pre-answer router can capture it: in a 0.5-7B pool the best K-way router recovered 7.5-14.4% of the gap. Treat oracle-gap numbers in routing papers as an upper bound, not a deployable gain.
contributions.evidence: §7.2, Table 3; Appendix J shows complementary coverage does not convert into router gain.

contributions.statement: Do not pick the best fixed model and evaluate a router against it on the same sample: the plug-in comparison is biased in a known direction.
contributions.evidence: Proposition 3 and Corollary 5; the pilot certified positive per-query opportunity on all three tasks under split selection but only HellaSwag survived selection-valid inference.

reason: The selection-valid evaluation protocol is new to the KB and applies to any team comparing routers, cascades or harness variants on a small task set. The empirical result comes from small open models on single-turn benchmarks, so transfer to coding-agent routing is indirect and strength stays moderate.
